newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Japanese rhetoric stems dollar surge.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Japanese rhetoric stems dollar surge.

text.p: The dollar is likely to have peaked just above 120 yen for now after a barrage of contradictory comments from Japan and fear of Bank of Japan (BOJ) intervention put dollar bulls on hold, analysts said on Friday.

"The sheer volume of comments from Japanese officials lately has introduced an element of doubt about Japan's willingness to let the dollar go much higher," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
But the trend for a weak yen is still intact as the Japanese economy remains fragile and domestic interest rates are expected to stay low.

The dollar hit a high of 120.15 yen on Friday, its highest level since February 1993, after Japanese officials said the weak yen did not have a major impact on Japan's economy and would not stall a recovery.
Foreign exchange traders saw the the comments as signalling that Japan might not stand in the way of a stronger dollar, traders said.

A flurry of dollar buying pushed the U.S. currency above 120 yen but it reversed below 119 yen soon after when a Ministry of Finance (MOF) official said the government did not want to see an excessively weak yen.
This contradictory remark came hot on the heels of rumours that the BOJ had sold dollars to stem the yen's sharp decline. Traders were sceptical though that the central bank intervened.
Analysts noted that it was unusal for Japan to mention a specific dollar/yen exchange rate. A Japanese government spokesman said he was confident the yen will not fall below 120 to the dollar.

"Japanese officials have made lots of comments about "excessive' yen weakness, but they never actually said what that meant," said Francis Breedon, foreign exchange strategist at Lehman Brothers. "Now that they mentioned 120, they will try very hard to protect it."

The dollar has now risen over 50 percent since hitting a post-war low in April 1995, with an accelerated rally of about five yen since early this year alone. Given the size and the speed of the rally, it is not surprising that it might take a breather now.

"The similarities are compelling. When the dollar dropped to its record low in 1995 you could not find a dollar bull anywhere. Now you can't find a bear, and that's usually when it gets hard to extend the upside," said Nick Parsons, FX strategist at Banque Paribas.
The dollar's sharp rise since the start of this year prompted many economists to raise their forecasts, with some predicting a rate of 125 to 130 yen by the middle of this year.
Analysts said the yen is likely to stabilise for now as evidence emerges that the Japanese economy is finally showing signs of life after years of stagnation after the 1980s asset bubble burst.

Housing starts and auto sales have risen sharply in the last six months. Exports are surging, helped by the competitive advantage of a weak yen. Employment is growing and consumer prices have firmed after a bout of deflation.

But as long as the U.S. economy powers ahead, expectations of interest rate rises there will continue to provide the dollar with firing power as Japanese investors seek higher yield outside Japan, analysts said.
And although the narrowing trend in Japan's trade surplus - a backbone of the dollar/yen rally - is coming to an end this does not mean the yen is about to embark on a rising trend.

U.S. officials, meanwhile, have supported a strong dollar along the way, and have toed that line even after the U.S. currency's latest surge. Their strong dollar stance has been echoed by other G7 nations.
Dealers will keep a close eye on a speech by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin later on Friday to gauge his reaction to the Japanese comments.
